The coda follows Maren down from the lighthouse and into the next morning.",
  "text": "Afterward, she stayed to put her glove on.

There was a split along the thumb. She had noticed it several nights before and forgotten it each morning. Now she held it against the window. A little harbour light showed through.

She went down carefully. Outside, the wind had dropped. Someone had left a bucket beneath the harbour tap, and water fell into it at long intervals. She walked past without stopping to tighten the tap.

At home she found the sewing tin behind the tea. Her mother had kept buttons in it, most of them belonging to clothes nobody owned now. Maren tipped a few into her palm while she looked for the needle.

She mended the glove with brown thread. The leather was black. In daylight the repair would show.

Then she went to bed.

In the morning there was bread on the step, wrapped in a clean cloth. No note. She brought it inside and cut two slices, though she was not especially hungry.

Erris passed the window on her way to school. She lifted one hand. Maren lifted hers, still holding the knife.

The girl stopped and pointed at the bread.

Maren opened the window.

"Your cloth?"

"My gran's. She wants it back."

"I'll wash it."

"She said you'd say that."

Erris ran to catch someone farther along the street.

Maren ate standing at the counter. Beyond the roofs, a boat was moving out between the harbour walls. She watched until it passed from sight, then rinsed the knife and laid the cloth beside the sink for washing."

  "text": "The cloth dried by noon. Maren folded it along the old creases and took it up the street.

Erris's grandmother was kneeling beside her gate, working a knife under a weed. She accepted the cloth without getting up.

"Good bread," Maren said.

"Better toasted tomorrow."

The woman put the cloth over her shoulder and returned to the weed. Maren held the gate steady while she hauled herself upright.

"Agnes used to lean on that," she said. "Nearly took it off its hinges."

Maren looked at the gate. One hinge had been replaced; the other was thick with green paint.

"That sounds like her."

"She said she'd mend it."

For a moment Maren wanted to promise that she would. Instead she smiled, and the old woman smiled too.

On the way home she bought potatoes, lamp oil, and black thread. The shopkeeper asked whether she wanted her mother's usual amount of oil.

"For now," she said.

She carried everything home in a box. Under the potatoes was a packet of flower seeds, its paper faded almost white. She had not asked for it. She set it on the windowsill, where she would see it again.

That evening she cooked too many potatoes. She put the extra ones aside for frying and sat down before her supper cooled.

At eleven she checked the weather from the doorstep. Rain was coming. She brought her coat near the stove and put the mended gloves in its pockets.

There was still time before she had to leave. She fetched her book and found her place."

  "text": "By spring she had finished the book. She disliked its ending and lent it to Erris, who brought it back a week later with the same complaint.

They planted the seeds in a shallow box because neither knew how tall the flowers would grow. Erris made holes with a pencil. Maren followed with the watering can, washing two seeds out of place.

"They won't mind," Erris said.

The box stood outside her kitchen door. For several mornings nothing happened. Then there were green hooks in the soil, so small that Maren knelt to see them.

Her nights continued. Some were wet, some clear. Once she climbed the lighthouse stairs angry about a bill; once with a tune in her head that would not leave. At ten past midnight she gave the brass clock its three turns. The work took the same time whether she dreaded it or scarcely thought of it.

In June, Erris's grandmother asked about the flowers.

"Yellow," Maren said. "That's all I know so far."

"Bring me one when they open."

The first opened on a Thursday. Maren fetched the scissors, then hesitated over the solitary head. She cut it with enough stem for a little bottle.

At the gate she found the old woman tightening the loose hinge. Maren held the screws in her palm and passed them over one at a time.

Afterward they sat in the kitchen. The flower stood between them in a bottle that had once held medicine.

"There," the old woman said, moving it out of her elbow's way. "Now. Will you have tea?""
